doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Meeting Bill Evans on the Staten Island ferry
summary: In the Bowery years he took a singer's quiet companion on a ferry ride and discovered he was pianist Bill Evans.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: The suits. They call them suits. The corporate treasury. Now that Jazz Workshop, that was the mid-’50s, ’55, ’56. What had been happening for you between the time you had gotten married, which I think you said was around ’53 and that point? Just maintaining? Or any . . . ?

Yeah, just writing at every opportunity. We got a – we managed to get a hotel in that one room upstairs. I remember one day a singer came to town. She had wanted me to do some arranging for her for a record. A very beautiful singer. But it was one of those Sundays in New York, summertime Sundays, when the city is really quiet and you try to think of what to do. She had a guy with her, a singer. I couldn’t think of anything to do, because he didn’t speak very much. So I said, “Let’s take the Staten Island ferry.” So Juanita and I and what’s-her-name – I’ll get that too – we went down and took the Staten Island ferry over and back. The guy didn’t talk very much. So I said – when we got through with the ride, I said, “Let’s go back home,” because he looked like a banker. That’s what he looked like, like a business banker. So I said, “What do you do?” “I play piano.” You know what happened next.
He sat down at the piano, and I felt like jumping up and saying hallelujah. It was Bill Evans.
The introspective one. He was truly that way. Who was the singer? You’ve really got me curious now. We have singers we associate you with, but obviously we’re not talking about any of them.
Okay. It’ll come to you. So you guys must have had a grand time at that point. He was soaking . . .
